Lecture 23

Discrete series and the rank one unitary picture

What this lecture does

We realise the holomorphic discrete series of SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R) on weighted spaces of holomorphic functions on the disk. We then compare it with the finite-dimensional and principal series modules, and a map UnU_nUn​ identifies its polynomials with a half-ladder of the principal series. Finally we state the full list of irreducible unitary representations, and we prove that a finite-dimensional unitary representation is trivial.

23.1 The disk model

A function on an open subset of the complex plane is holomorphic if it is complex differentiable at every point.

We import three results from elementary complex analysis. The first is the local power-series theorem. A holomorphic function on a disk has a Taylor series converging uniformly on every smaller closed disk. The second concerns power series. A power series about the centre of a disk that converges at every point of the disk defines a holomorphic function there. The third follows from the Cauchy–Riemann equations. The real Jacobian of a holomorphic map is the squared modulus of its complex derivative. These are the analytic inputs used below. See MIT 18.112, the lectures on Cauchy's formula, power series and the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

Proposition 23.15. Let VVV be an irreducible (g,K)(\g,K)(g,K)-module of GGG. Assume each KKK-type has multiplicity at most one and Ω\OmegaΩ acts by ccc. Suppose VVV has a positive definite inner product satisfying (23.7) for the module action. Proof. By (23.7) and (23.8), ∥Evk∥2=−⟨vk,FEvk⟩=14(k(k+2)−c)∥vk∥2\|Ev_k\|^2=-\langle v_k,FEv_k\rangle=\tfrac14(k(k+2)-c)\|v_k\|^2∥Evk​∥2=−⟨vk​,FEvk​⟩=41​(k(k+2)−c)∥vk​∥2. Since ∥Evk∥2\|Ev_k\|^2∥Evk​∥2 and ∥vk∥2\|v_k\|^2∥vk​∥2 are real and vk≠0v_k\ne0vk​=0, this identity shows that ccc is real.

By irreducibility, all KKK-types have the parity of kkk. Since EEE raises and FFF lowers KKK-types by 222, the span of the vjv_jvj​ with j≤kj\le kj≤k is invariant. It is nonzero and misses vk+2v_{k+2}vk+2​, which contradicts irreducibility. So (23.9) is strict.

For the lowest-weight pattern (i), Fvλ=0Fv_\lambda=0Fvλ​=0, so (23.8) gives c=λ(λ−2)c=\lambda(\lambda-2)c=λ(λ−2). Each entry is irreducible and unitary, and is determined by its KKK-types and its Casimir value ccc. For n≥2n\ge2n≥2 the last two rows are the discrete series. For n=1n=1n=1 they are the limits of discrete series, realised with the norm of Remark 23.11. Their sum is the odd principal series at c=−1c=-1c=−1.

The last column gives the parameters of Lecture 22 with c=ν2−1c=\nu^2-1c=ν2−1. In the principal and complementary rows the entry has the module Vε,νV_{\varepsilon,\nu}Vε,ν​, with ε=0\varepsilon=0ε=0 in the even rows and ε=1\varepsilon=1ε=1 in the odd row, and ν\nuν and −ν-\nu−ν give the same module. In the other rows the entry is only one piece of a reducible module Vε,νV_{\varepsilon,\nu}Vε,ν​. So a value of ν\nuν can carry several entries of the list.

Proposition 23.15 proves the necessity of the ccc-ranges for these KKK-type patterns. Call a (g,K)(\g,K)(g,K)-module even if its KKK-types are 2Z2\mathbb Z2Z, and odd if they are 2Z+12\mathbb Z+12Z+1. An irreducible even module with a positive definite inner product satisfying (23.7) needs c<0c<0c<0. The part c≤−1c\le-1c≤−1 is the unitary principal series of Lecture 22. The interval −1<c<0-1<c<0−1<c<0 is the complementary series. The inner product of the complementary series is fixed by (23.9), not by the L2L^2L2 norm of Lecture 22 (Exercise 23.5). An irreducible odd module with such an inner product needs c<−1c<-1c<−1, so there is no odd complementary series. At c=−1c=-1c=−1 the odd principal series module has FEv−1=0FEv_{-1}=0FEv−1​=0 and splits.

Figure 23.3 sets the list against ccc. We use ccc and not ν\nuν because of the last remark on the table. At c=−1c=-1c=−1 the odd principal series splits into Π1\Pi_1Π1​ and Π1−\Pi_1^-Π1−​. At c=0c=0c=0 the representations Π2\Pi_2Π2​, Π2−\Pi_2^-Π2−​ and the trivial representation are distinct.

The cited parts are the converse and the exhaustion. They use two results of Harish-Chandra (compare Lecture 21). First, every irreducible unitary representation is admissible. Its KKK-finite vectors form an irreducible (g,K)(\g,K)(g,K)-module with multiplicity-one KKK-types on which Ω\OmegaΩ is scalar. Second, each module above with an invariant positive definite Hermitian form integrates to an irreducible unitary representation of GGG. Etingof's MIT 18.757 notes treat admissibility in Lecture 5 and unitary globalisation in Theorem 7.5.

We can now explain the word discrete. For a compact group, the Plancherel theorem of Lecture 11 writes the squared norm of a function as a sum over the irreducible representations. For GGG the corresponding formula has a sum and integrals. Let hhh be smooth with compact support on GGG, and put Π(h)=∫Gh(g)Π(g) dg\Pi(h)=\int_Gh(g)\Pi(g)\,dgΠ(h)=∫G​h(g)Π(g)dg. For a suitable normalisation of Haar measure, h(I)=∫Rtr⁡Π0,iv(h) vtanh⁡πv2 dv+∫Rtr⁡Π1,iv(h) vcoth⁡πv2 dv+∑n≥24(n−1)tr⁡(Πn(h)+Πn−(h)).\begin{align*} h(I)={}&\int_{\R}\tr\Pi_{0,iv}(h)\,v\tanh\frac{\pi v}2\,dv+\int_{\R}\tr\Pi_{1,iv}(h)\,v\coth\frac{\pi v}2\,dv\\ &+\sum_{n\ge2}4(n-1)\tr\bigl(\Pi_n(h)+\Pi_n^-(h)\bigr). \end{align*}h(I)=​∫R​trΠ0,iv​(h)vtanh2πv​dv+∫R​trΠ1,iv​(h)vcoth2πv​dv+n≥2∑​4(n−1)tr(Πn​(h)+Πn−​(h)).​ We cite this inversion formula from Knapp, §II.7, formula (2.25), and we do not use it. Knapp proves it as Theorem 11.6 in §XI.3 and credits it to Harish-Chandra (1952). The Plancherel formula for GGG follows from it. The discrete series enters through a discrete sum, and the unitary principal series enters through integrals over ν=iv\nu=ivν=iv. Neither the complementary series nor Π1±\Pi_1^\pmΠ1±​ appears. The number n−1n-1n−1 is the one in Exercise 23.6, where the coefficient of e0e_0e0​ has squared norm C/(n−1)C/(n-1)C/(n−1).

Finally we return to finite dimensions. The next statement does not use Bargmann’s theorem, and it needs no irreducibility hypothesis.

Corollary 23.17. Every finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation Π\PiΠ of GGG is trivial.

Proof. By the theorem of Lecture 3 on continuous homomorphisms, Π\PiΠ is smooth. The complex-linear extension of dΠd\PidΠ makes the space VVV a finite-dimensional module of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C). The real element H0=diag⁡(1,−1)H_0=\diag(1,-1)H0​=diag(1,−1) is the diagonal element of the triple of Lecture 20. So complete reducibility and the highest-weight calculation of the prerequisite Lie Algebras course make dΠ(H0)d\Pi(H_0)dΠ(H0​) diagonalisable with integer eigenvalues. Unitarity makes the same operator skew-Hermitian, with imaginary eigenvalues. Therefore dΠ(H0)=0d\Pi(H_0)=0dΠ(H0​)=0.

The kernel of the complexified differential is an ideal of sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C) containing the nonzero element H0H_0H0​. Since sl(2,C)\sllie(2,\C)sl(2,C) is simple, this kernel is everything, so dΠ=0d\Pi=0dΠ=0. Since GGG is connected, it is generated by exponentials (Lecture 2), and Π(exp⁡X)=exp⁡dΠ(X)=I\Pi(\exp X)=\exp d\Pi(X)=IΠ(expX)=expdΠ(X)=I. Hence Π\PiΠ is trivial. 

So a nontrivial unitary representation of GGG is infinite-dimensional. Exercise 23.3 checks this directly for the finite-dimensional modules Π−d\Pi_{-d}Π−d​ of Example 23.12(ii).

23.6 Summary

For each integer n≥2n\ge2n≥2, formula (23.5) defines an irreducible unitary representation Πn\Pi_nΠn​ on An\mathcal A_nAn​. Its KKK-types are n,n+2,…n,n+2,\dotsn,n+2,…, each once. The operator EEE raises the KKK-type by 222 and FFF lowers it by 222. The Casimir element Ω\OmegaΩ acts by n(n−2)n(n-2)n(n−2). The relation k2π=Ik_{2\pi}=Ik2π​=I forces integral KKK-types. The representation Πn\Pi_nΠn​ descends to PSL(2,R)\mathrm{PSL}(2,\R)PSL(2,R) exactly for even nnn. In an irreducible unitary module with KKK-types λ,λ+2,…\lambda,\lambda+2,\dotsλ,λ+2,…, the lowest weight is an integer λ≥1\lambda\ge1λ≥1, and Ω\OmegaΩ acts by λ(λ−2)\lambda(\lambda-2)λ(λ−2). Positivity of ∥Evk∥2\|Ev_k\|^2∥Evk​∥2 explains the shape of Bargmann's cited list, including the complementary series.

The map UnU_nUn​ carries the polynomials of Πn\Pi_nΠn​ onto the half-ladder k≥nk\ge nk≥n of the principal series at ν=n−1\nu=n-1ν=n−1, and only the norm differs. For n=1n=1n=1 the norms agree, and this constructs Π1\Pi_1Π1​ as a summand of the odd principal series at ν=0\nu=0ν=0. Every finite-dimensional continuous unitary representation of GGG is trivial. We also cited the inversion formula for GGG, whose discrete sum runs over the discrete series.

23.7 Reading

  • A. W. Knapp, Representation Theory of Semisimple Groups: An Overview Based on Examples, Princeton University Press, 2001 edition. §VI.1 treats the holomorphic discrete series of SU⁡(1,1)\SU(1,1)SU(1,1). §§II.5–II.6 treat the unitary representations of SL⁡(2,R)\SL(2,\R)SL(2,R). §II.7 states the inversion formula cited above, and §XI.3 proves it.

  • MIT 18.112, Functions of a Complex Variable, Fall 2008: Cauchy's formula, power series and the Cauchy–Riemann equations.

  • P. Etingof, Representations of Lie Groups, MIT 18.757 lecture notes, Fall 2023. Lecture 5 treats admissibility, and Theorem 7.5 is the unitary globalisation theorem.

  • Harish-Chandra, Plancherel formula for the 2×22\times22×2 real unimodular group, Proc. Nat. Acad. Sci. USA 38 (1952), 337–342.

  • V. Bargmann, Irreducible unitary representations of the Lorentz group, Ann. of Math. 48 (1947), 568–640, for the original classification.
